\subsection{Numerical implementation}
The discretized equations are solved using a combination of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and a time-evolution algorithm based on the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. The FFT is used to efficiently calculate the discrete Laplacian and the discrete curl, which are needed for the kinetic energy and magnetic field energy terms, respectively. The Runge-Kutta method is used to advance the system in time, with a time step $\Delta t$ chosen to ensure numerical stability. The Josephson term is implemented using the discretized form derived above, and the total energy of the system is calculated as the sum of the kinetic energy, magnetic field energy, and Josephson energy terms. The system is initialized with random phases and vector potentials, and the evolution is monitored over time to observe the formation of patterns and the emergence of dynamical behavior. The periodic boundary conditions ensure that the system remains finite and well-defined, and the isotropic grid spacing ensures that the discretization is uniform in all directions. The numerical results are validated by comparing them to analytical solutions in the limit of small grid spacing $h$ and by checking the conservation of energy throughout the simulation.

The characteristic equations can be used to identify multiply imaged arclets. 
For a given $\mu$-field, the characteristics are the curves along which the 
source plane is mapped onto the deflector plane. If the source is extended,

All Lie algebras considered in this paper are finite-dimensional over the field $F$ and are soluble. The
theory of saturated formations and of $\fF$-projectors was developed in Barnes and Gastineau-Hills

definition of intravariance for subalgebras of Lie algebras was given in Barnes \cite{Frat}.

\begin{Definition}  The subalgebra $U$ of the Lie algebra $L$ is said to be
{\em intravariant} in $L$ if every derivation of $L$ is expressible as the sum of an inner
derivation and a derivation which stabilises $U$.  \end{Definition}

By \cite[Lemma 1.2]{Frat}, the intravariant subalgebras of $L$ are precisely those subalgebras $U$ with
the property that, if $L$ is an ideal of $L^*$, then $L^* = L + \sN_{L^*}(U)$. It was proved in 
\cite[Theorem 2.2]{Frat} that, if $\fF$ is a saturated formation of soluble Lie algebras, then the
$\fF$-projectors of a soluble Lie algebra $L$ are intravariant in $L$. It seems reasonable to
conjecture that the $\fF$-normalisers also are intravariant. The following definitions are taken from
Stitzinger \cite{Stit}.

\begin{Definition}  A maximal subalgebra $M$ of $L$ is called $\fF$-normal if it
complements an $\fF$-central chief factor of $L$. Equivalently, $M$ is
$\fF$-normal if for some chief factor $A/B$ of $L$, $M+A = L$ and the split

is, if $L/\core(M) \notin \fF$. \end{Definition}

is $\fF$-abnormal and $M + N(L) = L$ where $N(L)$ is the nil radical of $L$. \end{Definition}
